text.p: VIENNA, July 18 (Reuter) The main stories in the Austrian press this Friday are:
DER STANDARD

- Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger has drawn up a budget for 1998 whose deficit complies with the Maastricht criteria. With income of 682 billion schillings and spending of 749.3 billion, the budget foresees a net deficit of 67.3 billion -- or 2.6 percent of gross domestic product.
- German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Italy's Prime Minister Romano Prodi and Chancellor Viktor Klima agree at the Schengen summit in Innsbruck to open Austria's borders from spring 1998 onwards.
- Unemployment in Austria's construction industry hit a record high in June with 21,000 unemployed, a seven percent increase on June 1996.
DIE PRESSE
- Joining the Schengen group will cost Austria around 2.733 billion schillings to the year 2000 as it must secure around 1,460 kilometres of the EU's outer borders.
- Interior Minister Karl Schloegl insists Austria is not forcing the repatriation of Bosnian refugees like Germany and Switzerland.
- The budget for 1998 has not put aside any money for economic research.
- The EU will pay back 1.6 billion schillings to Austria for 1996.
WIRTSCHAFTS BLATT

- Austrian Airlines' deal with Lauda Air has brought shareholders 2.4 billion schillings so far. AUA's chairman expects synergies to bring a 200 percent increase in earnings this year to 300 million schillings.
SALZBURGER NACHRICHTEN
- The Vienna ATX index reached a new high, closing at 1429,29.
- Verbund's committee demands an open invitation of tenders should the government sell its 25 percent stake in the national grid company.
- More than 95 percent of businesses in Austria have made no preparations for EMU, according to a study by the economics ministry.
KURIER
- Siemens has been criticised by a union for threatening to close its Austrian cable operation unless the entire workforce accepts a 13 percent pay cut.
- Three Austrian banks have been awarded prizes by the British economics magazine Euromoney, namely CA, RZB and BA.
- The two bidders for Austria's third GSM license, Connect Austria and Orange Telekom, are both prepared to pay up to four billion schillings for it, according to company insiders.
- Apprentice training is too expensive for firms, according to a study.
- The dilemma of the wine economy: sweet grapes, sour balances.
